entry.summary: There's a good chance you are not getting the best out of your LLM (Large Language Model) not because the model isn't powerful enough, but because your prompt isn't. Maybe you are too quick to ask a question before structuring your thought or it could be that you are not giving your LLM enough context. In my early days of writing prompts, I found myself doing something interestingly odd which is giving my rough prompt to another LLM just to see how it would rewrite or improve it and most times the results are often better, more structured and often closer to what I actually needed. At the time, I didn’t have a name for this process. It just felt like I was refining a prompt through another prompt. But few weeks ago, I learned the actual term which is called meta prompting. entry.title: How Code Goes from Your Local Machine to a Live App
entry.summary:
Here’s a quick breakdown of what a typical Azure DevOps pipeline looks like — straight from commit to production:
Run basic checks — linting, build, unit tests. If something fails, no merge. Keeps bad code out early. Once merged, CI kicks in. It runs integration tests, pulls secrets from Azure Key Vault, and builds the container image. Keeps the codebase stable. Deploy to staging (e.g., AKS). Run acceptance tests. Add a manual approval step if needed. Make sure everything works before going live. If staging is green, promote the image to production. No rebuilds. No surprises. Use Azure Monitor + Container Insights for logs, metrics, health checks. Application Insights helps debug real issues fast. Defender for DevOps helps with static code analysis and pipeline-level security. Set it up once — saves you later. That’s it — a reliable, secure pipeline from PR to production. entry.title: Google AI Studio Challenge - Linux Services Monitor
entry.summary:
My Linux Services Monitor (Simulated) – Built with Google AI Studio Prompt: Build a simple web app using vanilla JavaScript, HTML, and CSS called "My Linux Services Monitor." It should display a list of fake Linux services like ssh, cron, and cups. Each service should have a randomly assigned status: "Running," "Stopped," or "Failed." Use a button labeled “Refresh Status” that re-randomizes all the statuses. Use color-coded labels or icons to indicate each status (green = running, gray = stopped, red = failed). Keep the UI clean, readable, and beginner-friendly. No backend, no frameworks, no TypeScript. AI Studio created the html, css and js code.
It displays a list of common system services (like sshd, cron, cupsd, etc.) along with their current status: Running, Stopped, or Failed. A refresh button lets you simulate status updates, randomly changing the state of each service. Important: This is a mock simulator, not connected to an actual Linux system. The status of each service is randomized with each refresh to demonstrate layout, interactivity, and dynamic behavior in a web app. The purpose of this project was to test what Google AI Studio could generate from a natural-language prompt — and to explore how it could help someone without a programming background (like myself) spin up functional web UI quickly. A fully working version would require additional development — specifically a backend component to read real system data (via systemctl or similar) and pass it to the frontend securely. Still, as a learning tool and a prototype, this shows how far you can go with AI-assisted code generation using only a prompt. I think this was the goal of the challenge. I'm a retired electronics tech and programming is my avocation — if I can get this far with Gemini AI Studio, anyone can.
